extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists and serial fiction writers (creative writers)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical craft and professional principles for writing novels, serial fiction, and related literary/reporting work — covering habits of composition, character consistency, serial-publication strategy, realism, setting, illustration collaboration, and professional conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write final-form reports without drafts
rubrics_metrics.description: Habit of writing reports in the form in which they should be sent, --without a copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By writing thus a man can throw on to his paper the exact feeling with which his mind is impressed at the moment. A rough copy, or that which is called a draft, is written in order that it may be touched and altered and put upon stilts. The waste of time in such an operation is terrible. If a man knows his craft with his pen, he will have learned to write without the necessity of changing his words or the form of his sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obey authority promptly but speak your opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Always obey authority in everything instantly, but never allow your mouth to be closed as to the expression of your opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When carrying out instructions which you know should not have been given, point out the fatuity of the improper order in the strongest language you can decently employ. Distinguishes compliance in action from suppression of professional judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep control of the whole work before publishing parts
rubrics_metrics.description: An artist should keep in his hand the power of fitting the beginning of his work to the end; no part of a novel should be published till the entire story was completed (principle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serial publication (sending small parts hot to press) is injurious because it removes the author's ability to remedy defects and to make the beginning fit the end. The principle may be superseded for a just occasion ('if the reason be "tanti," the principle should for the occasion be put in abeyance'), but breaking it should be exceptional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain unbroken character consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Servetur ad imum — Your Achilles should all through, from beginning to end, be 'impatient, fiery, ruthless, keen.' Your Achilles... will probably keep up his character. But your Davus also should be always Davus, and that is more difficult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure each character remains true to the traits established at first; if you make an early portrait (e.g., angelic purity), be prepared to tone down later elements rather than have inconsistent conduct. This is especially important when serialising or when revising earlier passages after later development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve the power to remedy defects
rubrics_metrics.description: The writer should keep in his hands the power of remedying any defect in this respect (fitting beginning to end).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when publishing in parts, retain the ability to correct or adjust earlier material to maintain coherence; avoid committing irrevocably to early lines that later prove incompatible with developments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid tediousness in serial instalments
rubrics_metrics.description: The production of novels in serial form forces upon the author the conviction that he should not allow himself to be tedious in any single part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A serial-writer cannot afford many pages to be skipped by readers at any one time; each installment should engage and avoid long successions of dull pages or 'bathos of dulness.' Recognize the heightened need for pacing and interest in each published segment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent characters as realistic, not exaggerated
rubrics_metrics.description: Make men and women walk upon it just as they do walk here among us,--with not more of excellence, nor with exaggerated baseness,--so that my readers might recognise human beings like to themselves, and not feel themselves to be carried away among gods or demons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for believable, ordinary human characterisation so readers can identify and learn moral lessons from them; avoid creating figures so elevated or debased that readers cannot relate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use fiction to teach virtue accessibly
rubrics_metrics.description: Regard my art as a preacher of sermons, and my pulpit as one which I could make both salutary and agreeable to my audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convey moral lessons (e.g., honesty, modesty, truth) through representations of ordinary characters so that the 'hasty normal reader' can grasp and be influenced by them; novels may reach readers who won't read higher poetry or philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborate with illustrators who subordinate to the author's intent
rubrics_metrics.description: An artist can either make a pretty picture, or study the work of the author from whose writing he was bound to take his subject. It was his object to promote the views of the writer whose work he had undertaken to illustrate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer illustrators who study and serve the author's ideas rather than those who produce prettiness that contradicts or ignores the text. The good illustrator will subordinate personal whim and spare no pains to understand the author's intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know your setting intimately (make a map)
rubrics_metrics.description: As I wrote it I became more closely than ever acquainted with the new shire which I had added to the English counties... I had it all in my mind,--its roads and railroads, its towns and parishes, its members of Parliament... I made a map of the dear county.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop a detailed mental (or literal) map of the setting so that every fictitious site represents a spot the author knows thoroughly; this lends authenticity and consistency across works.

rubrics_metrics.name: It is possible to write multiple works concurrently
rubrics_metrics.description: When I had half-finished Framley Parsonage, I went back to my other story... This was the only occasion on which I have had two different novels in my mind at the same time. Many of us live in different circles... I do not see why two or three should not be well written at the same time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With acquired craft an author can keep different tales distinct and work on more than one project simultaneously; trust the process and allow the mind to work on completed material while composing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust composition over preplanning
rubrics_metrics.description: I have never found myself thinking much about the work that I had to do till I was doing it. I have indeed for many years almost abandoned the effort to think, trusting myself, with the narrowest thread of a plot, to work the matter out when the pen is in my hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on active composition to develop detail and resolution rather than exhaustive pre-planning; keep a slender plot outline and let the writing itself elaborate scenes and character development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared to set aside personal principles for just causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Such a principle becomes a tyrant if it cannot be superseded on a just occasion. If the reason be 'tanti,' the principle should for the occasion be put in abeyance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain craft principles, but exercise judgement; exceptional circumstances (financial, editorial, practical) may justify breaking a self-imposed rule — do so sparingly and with deliberate choice.
